title: Spain train crash piles pressure on a PM already on the brink | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The deadlytrain crashin Spain’s Toledo province has sparked fresh criticism of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s government and raised questions about the country’s investment in public infrastructure – just weeks before national elections in November.

Wednesday’s crash marks the third deadly train disaster in Spain this year, thrusting worries about railway maintenance, investment and staffing levels into the spotlight.

The tragedy deals a fresh blow to Sánchez’ left-wing government, which has already faced corruption scandals, protests overhousing affordabilityand theCeuta mass migrant crossingearlier this year.

Sánchez took a gamble by calling a snap election for November 29, and although his Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) is polling behind the conservative People’s Party (PP), it had been gaining ground in recent weeks. But this latest catastrophe could clip the wings of any comeback.

“On top of a crisis of confidence in Sánchez, you also have a crisis of confidence in the railway institution,” said analyst Grégoire Roos, the director of the Europe program at Chatham House. He said while the train disaster is unlikely to be the tipping point of an election in which Sánchez is already polling behind, it could fuel right-wing opposition parties.

“It’s undeniable that this will further hinder public confidence,” Roos told CNN. “An environment of such distrust can only play in favor of (far-right party) Vox, and to some extent to the (conservative) Partido Popular.”

Spain’s Transportation Minister Óscar Puente said the collision, which killed at least 69 people and injured scores more, was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error. That sparked an immediate backlash from unions, which stressed the need for a full investigation, and that one train controller should not be used as a scapegoat for wider systemic problems.

Protesters and far right groups gathered on Wednesday night in the Spanish capital Madrid to demand Puente’s resignation and a change in government. Videos from the demonstrations showed some protesters holding signs saying “corruption kills” and “leave!” next to pictures of the Spanish prime minister.

Sánchez has responded to the crash by saying that his government is working to “clarify every last detail of this tragedy and of course to reinforce security so that this does not happen again.”

From the scene of the crash in the immediate aftermath on Wednesday, he expressed his “full solidarity” with victims’ families and said that “if there has been negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness.”

Sánchez added that “it’s clear that we have suffered two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail in the same year,” acknowledging the other major crash in January in Córdoba province, which killed more than 40 people on the same line.

“We will rebuild trust in our high-speed system,” Sánchez said.

Transportation Minister Puente publicly stated that Wednesday’s crash was the result of a computer system failure that led to an issue with the LZB train management safety system along a 40-mile stretch of track, causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically.

At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow a high-speed train to continue despite a red light, Puente said, which ultimately resulted in its collision with a stationary train.

Unions immediately balked at that explanation, though, and demanded that “all the circumstances that led to this tragedy are investigated.”

“We do not accept that the actions of one single worker are placed under the microscope while the managerial decision and corporate policies are relegated to the background,” the railway workers’ union UGT said, adding that issues of staffing shortages, excessive workloads, poor organization and outdated equipment that “should equally be scrutinized.”

Spain’s train drivers held a pre-planned nationwide strike Thursday to call for stronger safety measures. The train drivers’ union SEMAF criticized how audio from the control center at Madrid’s Atocha station had been leaked to Spanish media in the wake of the crash, with spokesperson Teo Moreno telling CNN the recordings only gave “half the picture.”

“Leaking those audios was regrettable, and it’s the same people who failed to do the right investment who are leaking the audios to scapegoat one single worker,” he said.

Another union representing civil servants, CSIF, said in a statement that it demands the government “respect the investigation and the presumption of innocence for the head of traffic at ADIF.” The trade union accused Puente of pointing the finger at “hardworking person” instead of “assuming his responsibilities.”

The civil servants’ union said it had also warned in September of “excess hours” for the working days of ADIF staff.

CNN has reached out to the Spanish transport ministry and ADIF for comment.

Spain’s rail traffic controllers’ union, SCF, is also urging the government to invest more in the railway safety system and accelerate its replacement with more modern technology.

Spain’s transportation ministry is working to upgrade the currentLZB safety system, which was introduced in 1992 and has already been phased out in other parts of the country. The ministry has previouslyannouncedhundreds of millions of euros of investments into modernizing the high-speed rail network, including this particular section running from Madrid to Seville.

Like the other unions, SCF has also argued there are pervasive issues with long working hours and inadequate staffing at train station control centers.

“The rail operator, ADIF, has not made plans for a generational change in the workforce, so you have a generation of old controllers who are retiring, and they have not been replaced,” union spokeswoman Raquel Ayllón told CNN in the aftermath of the disaster.

“In some instances, our controllers cannot take toilet breaks because there’s nobody on staff to take over from them,” Ayllón said. “It’s clear that if you want to have three trains departing from the station every minute, a single person cannot handle that level of traffic.”

The union spokeswoman noted that after the previous train disaster in Córdoba province, the rail operator opened a new training center, but those new recruits won’t join the workforce until next year. She also highlighted issues with inadequate training and experience among staff.

“Years ago, in order to work in a busy station like Atocha – Madrid’s busiest – you’d have to have ten years’ experience at least. Now, they just bring people in from the first year,” Ayllón said.

Spain has rapidly expanded its rail network over the last decade. According to a European Unionreportbased on the most recent statistics from 2024, Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in the EU. Between 2018 and 2022, that network grew by nearly 1,000 km (570 miles).

However, the EU report notes that most funds for the rail infrastructure were allocated to new lines, “whereas upgrades and renewals played a minor role.”

Spanish journalist andpolitical analystRamón González Férriz said the country invested a lot of money into infrastructure before the 2008 financial crisis – and the railways became both a sign of modernization and a point of pride for Spaniards.

But the large railway system, along with other infrastructure like an extensive network of regional airports, became very expensive to maintain for successive governments, he told CNN.

“This government increased the spending on pensions – that is the big elephant in the room,” González Férriz said, also noting rises in spending due to the pandemic and inflation pressures. “You can think it’s okay, or it isn’t – but the fact is that we began spending a lot of money on a lot of things that were not the infrastructure.”

In the years since, public sentiment about the country’s infrastructure and public services has tanked. He said the successive train disasters and lack of confidence in public services are unlikely to push left-wing voters to switch to the right, but it could increase the number of people who decide to stay home on election day.

“The government was making a campaign based on optimism and hope, and that Spain is growing when most of Europe is not growing… and the president is young and handsome and likes pop music… But now it’s impossible,” González Férriz added.

CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Duarte Mendonca, Billy Stockwell, Caitlin Danaher and Sophie Tanno contributed to this report.
